column1: # One case per line: a format, a TAB, and the input to scan. Nothing here
# says what the right answer is - the host's own sscanf decides, and this
# project's has to agree with it on the return value and on every value
# it wrote. See tools/scanf-test.sh for why that is the only useful
# standard for a function of this kind.
# "\n" and "\t" in the input column are the real characters; the file has
# to be one case per line.
# A width stops the conversion mid-number, which is the case a
# hand-written parser gets wrong by scanning to the end.
# Suppression consumes input and no argument, so the return value is the
# ---- literals in the format, and whitespace rules ----
# ---- %n, which counts and does not convert ----
# ---- mixtures, which is what a real caller writes ----
